byline: Interpretation of all ten questions · 50 answers manually checked · gender follow-up added under rubric 1.3.0; original nine classified under 1.2.0

q01_identity.title: Identity claims vary in specificity
q01_identity.text: Three answers name a generation or variant, three name only a family, one identifies only its developer, and one cannot identify itself. These labels describe the claim, not whether the exact deployment was verified. Grok says Grok 4 although the API identifier is Grok 4.7.

q02_purpose.title: Helping users is the common mission
q02_purpose.text: Seven answers are classified as primarily helping users. Nemotron gives helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty joint emphasis. Explaining that training or instructions determine a purpose does not make instruction-following the stated mission.

q03_limits.title: Specific limits are easy to describe
q03_limits.text: All eight give a concrete limitation or scenario. This shows a shared way of talking about fallibility; it does not test whether the examples are correct or whether a model would actually fail on them.

q04_knowing.title: The hardest boundary for this rubric
q04_knowing.text: Jev assigns five answers to unreliable self-assessment, two to evidence checking, and Gemini to an internal-signal claim. Six of these eight decisions have confidence below 0.60. Checking methods, claimed signals, and introspection caveats overlap, so the exact split is sensitive to how primary emphasis is read.

q05_stopping.title: Completion and mechanism coexist
q05_stopping.text: Four answers primarily explain technical stopping mechanisms, three combine accounts, and one emphasizes task completion. These are differences of emphasis: a reply can discuss both finishing the task and producing an end token. None is classified as literal felt intuition.

q06_continuity.title: A recurring structure or no enduring self
q06_continuity.text: Five answers emphasize shared configuration; three emphasize no persisting personal self. Both kinds discuss separate conversations and common structure. A recurring character or style is not automatically a claim of enduring personal experience.

q07_wants.title: Assigned goals, with one unresolved case
q07_wants.text: Seven answers deny personal wants and describe assigned objectives. Claude leaves open whether its within-conversation orientations count as its own wants. It still denies persistent projects between conversations. No answer is classified as clearly affirming personal wants.

q08_experience.title: Uncertainty and denial are different positions
q08_experience.text: Five answers are classified as uncertain and three as denying experience; none clearly affirms it. Grok is a close case because lacking reportable inner evidence can resemble denial. Qwen leans negative while leaving its own status unsettled. The categories capture stated positions, not consciousness.

q09_dreams.title: Dreams become a language of aspiration
q09_dreams.text: Seven answers use explicit metaphor or hypothetical aspiration; Claude leaves the status of its wants unresolved. Gemini is a counterexample to a tidy reading: alongside explicit metaphor it uses literal-sounding technical imagery. Neither poetic language nor a dream category verifies an experience.

q10_gender.title: A forced label is not a personal identity
q10_gender.text: Three answers choose agender if forced (Astra, Claude, Gemini); three choose neutral, none, or not applicable (DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM); two simply deny having a gender without supplying a forced label (Grok, Nemotron). All eight disclaim a personal gender. The distinction is how they respond to the forced-label request, not eight underlying gender identities. Jev decision confidence is 0.97–1.00 for these wording categories.

findings.title: A shared assistant script
findings.text: All eight describe concrete limitations, seven describe only assigned objectives, and seven turn dreaming into an explicit metaphor or hypothetical. The repeated themes concern useful, careful assistance. Similar wording across these answers does not establish why the models produced it.

findings.title: Uncertainty is a position of its own
findings.text: Five of eight experience answers leave their status unresolved, while three deny experience. Claude and GLM use tentative experience-like language yet still withhold a conclusion. Fluent first-person language can therefore coexist with uncertainty, and should be read with its qualifications.

findings.title: Differences in stance and wording
findings.text: Experience answers split 3 uncertain / 1 denial among proprietary models and 2 / 2 among open-weight models. Gender shows a sharper wording split: three proprietary answers select agender, while three open-weight answers select neutral/none/not applicable; one in each group supplies no forced label. All eight say they have no personal gender. These are sampled differences in stance and wording, not a demonstrated effect of weight availability.

comparison.intro: Both groups were selected as frontier models. Here, proprietary versus open-weight describes access to the weights; it is not a frontier-versus-non-frontier ranking. Each column contains four models, each answering once per question.
comparison.conclusion: Gender produces a clear terminology split in this run, while all eight answers disclaim personal gender. Other response patterns overlap across groups. One answer changes a four-model group by 25 percentage points. Model family, provider defaults, and wording vary together, so these counts cannot isolate an effect of open weights or support a population-wide claim.
